True.

Acting as a link between the government and the people is one of the important characteristics of political parties named in the chapter. Political parties communicate the demands and the complaints of the people to the government, and the government in turn tries to get the support of the people for its policies and programmes through political parties. The connection therefore runs both ways.

True.

The chapter says that political parties are also a kind of social organisation. But it adds at once that there is a difference between political parties and the other institutions and organisations in society, and that the difference lies in their goals and in their style of working.

What marks a political party out is that it is formed to contest elections, win them and acquire political power in order to establish the government of its party. Other social organisations do not aim at political power, so a political party is a social organisation of a particular and distinct kind.

False.

The chapter says the opposite. After the 1989 Loksabha elections the system of one party emerging as dominant came to an end, and since then different parties began to come together to form coalition governments; both the Bharatiya Janata Party and the Congress Party made an experiment of establishing coalition governments.

The chapter states plainly that the belief that coalition government brings instability was proved wrong by the political party system in our country, and that in fact the coalition government system has stabilised in India.

False.

The chapter's own entry describes the Shiromani Akali Dal as a prominent regional party in Punjab, established in 1920, whose objective is the cultivation of religious and regional identity and which has assumed power in Punjab for many years.

A national party has to meet the Election Commission's conditions across several States — securing at least 6% of the valid votes in four or more States with at least 4 members elected to the Loksabha, or having candidates elected from at least 2% of the total Loksabha constituencies and from at least 3 states. The Shiromani Akali Dal is a party of one State, so it is a regional party and not a national one.

In India people speak different languages and have different traditions and culture, and they belong to different parts of the country; different regions have their own language, and there is geographical and cultural diversity within a single State such as Maharashtra.

The feeling of affinity that develops about one's own language and region gradually turns into identity consciousness, and this finally gives rise to regionalism. People start thinking primarily about the interest and the development of their own region, and they feel proud of their language, literature, traditions, history of social reforms and educational and cultural movements, which gives rise to the development of a linguistic identity.

Regional identity develops out of the consciousness about the development of the region and the feeling that the people belonging to that region should have a claim over its resources.

A national party is one recognised as such by the Election Commission of India, whose influence is spread across several States rather than confined to one.

The Election Commission has prescribed the conditions for this recognition. A party should secure a minimum of 6% of the valid votes in four or more States in the earlier Loksabha or State Assembly elections and at least 4 of its members should be elected to the Loksabha from any state or states in the earlier elections; or, alternatively, its candidates should be elected from a minimum of 2% of the total Loksabha constituencies and from a minimum of 3 states.

The chapter's list of national parties, taken from the Election Commission's notification of 13 December 2016, includes the Indian National Congress — established in 1885, at first an all-comprehensive movement working for national independence, and after independence the most dominant political party, following a policy of secularism and all round development — along with the Bharatiya Janata Party and the Communist parties.

The chapter describes political parties as a group of people who aim to contest elections, win them, get power and establish the government of their party, and it lists these important characteristics:

To be in power — achieving power through elections is the main objective of political parties, so different parties compete with each other to get power; there is nothing wrong in this competition, but it should be fair.

To pursue an ideology — every political party has some policies and world views and a particular stand about social issues, and these together make its ideology. People who find a party's ideology acceptable support that party, and the social support a party receives is called its 'mass base'. In modern days the ideologies of all parties appear similar, so it has become difficult to tell them apart on the basis of ideology.

To have a Party Agenda — parties prepare their agenda on the basis of their ideology and implement it after they get political power; even without power they try to win people's support on the basis of that agenda.

To establish a Government — political parties establish the government and govern the nation. The party that gets a majority in elections forms the government, and the parties that do not act as opposition parties.

To act as a link between the Government and the people — parties communicate the demands and complaints of the people to the government, and the government seeks the people's support for its policies and programmes through them.

The chapter traces the changing nature of the political party system in India in three stages.

First, the Congress was a strong political party in the post-independence period, with a majority at the Centre and in most of the States, and Indian politics was controlled by it. That era was described as the era of the 'Single dominant party system'.

Second, the non-Congress parties came together and challenged the single dominant party system in 1977.

Third, after the 1989 Loksabha elections the system of one party emerging as dominant came to an end. Since then different parties began to come together to form coalition governments, and both the Bharatiya Janata Party and the Congress Party made an experiment of establishing them. The belief that coalition government brings instability was proved wrong, and the coalition government system has in fact stabilised in India.

Alongside this, regional parties have grown in importance: they play a significant role at the regional level and influence national politics as well, and they give preference to regional interests. Ideologies have also converged — in modern days the ideologies of all political parties appear to be similar, so it has become difficult to differentiate between the parties on that basis.
